what_its_for: Telotristat ethyl is used to treat diarrhea caused by carcinoid syndrome — a condition that happens when certain tumors (called carcinoid tumors) release too much of a chemical called serotonin into your body. This medicine works alongside other treatments called somatostatin analogs (such as octreotide or lanreotide) when those medicines alone are not fully controlling your diarrhea.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Taking it with a meal helps your body absorb the medicine better and may reduce stomach upset. Try to take it at the same times each day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual adult dose is one 250 mg tablet taken three times a day with meals (for example, with breakfast, lunch, and dinner). Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be adjusted based on your health and how you respond to the medicine. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular scheduled time with your next meal. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for the one you missed. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Store it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping meals when taking this medicine, since it needs food to work best. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because telotristat ethyl can interact with many other drugs, including certain heart medications, blood thinners, seizure medications, and antidepressants. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: severe constipation or no bowel movements for several days; stomach pain or cramping that is new or getting worse; nausea or vomiting that is severe or does not go away; signs of depression such as feeling very sad, hopeless, or having thoughts of harming yourself; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); or any new or unusual symptoms that concern you. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room if you feel like harming yourself.
when_it_works: You may start to notice fewer bowel movements and less diarrhea within the first few weeks of treatment. However, it may take up to 12 weeks to see the full benefit. Keep taking the medicine as directed even if you do not feel an immediate improvement. Talk to your doctor if your diarrhea is not improving after a few weeks.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): This medicine can generally be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you more closely. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose — make sure your doctor knows about any kidney issues. Liver problems: If you have moderate or severe liver disease, your dose may need to be lowered. Tell your doctor about any liver problems before starting this medicine. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine in children has not been established.
